summary: Redefines the DNS Authenticated Data (AD) bit. Based on implementation experience, the original meaning from RFC 2535 turned out to be not useful. It becomes set only when all answers, or the records proving no answers exist, were cryptographically verified or meet the server's local security policy. It has been replaced by RFCs 4033, 4034 and 4035.

eli5.summary: A checkmark on a DNS answer says it was checked. This made the checkmark mean something clearer and safer. Newer DNSSEC documents, RFCs 4033 to 4035, have since replaced it.

subtitle: Clarifying what the DNS Authenticated Data bit actually means.

tldr.problem: The Authenticated Data (AD) bit in DNS responses, as defined in RFC 2535, was not useful in practice: it only indicated that the server claimed to have authenticated data according to its policy, even if the data was not cryptographically verified.
tldr.mechanism: This specification redefines the AD bit to be set only when all answer data and any negative-proof data in the response has been cryptographically verified or meets the server's local security policy. Recursive servers set it after DNSSEC verification; authoritative servers rarely set it.
tldr.outcome: The AD bit now provides meaningful security information about whether DNS answers have been verified via DNSSEC. It was later superseded by RFCs 4033, 4034 and 4035, which provide the modern DNSSEC framework.

facts.label: When set
facts.value: All answer and proof data cryptographically verified

today: RFC 3655 has been superseded by RFC 4033, RFC 4034, and RFC 4035, which together define the modern DNSSEC framework. The AD bit interpretation defined here remains relevant for DNSSEC-aware applications.

sections.title: The Authenticated Data Bit Problem
sections.content:
The DNS Authenticated Data bit, defined in RFC 2535, was meant to indicate that all data in a DNS response had been authenticated by the server. However, the original definition had a practical flaw: a conformant server should never return data that failed its security policy, so the bit was not useful for distinguishing verified responses from unverified ones.

The new definition clarifies the bit's meaning: it is set only when all answer data, and any records proving that no answers exist, have been cryptographically verified via DNSSEC signatures or meet the server's local security policy. This makes the bit meaningful for applications that need to know whether their DNS answers are actually secure.
sections.eli5: The old checkmark could mean the server 'says' it checked things. The new one means it 'actually' checked the signatures to prove it.

sections.title: Why This Matters
sections.content:
A full DNSSEC resolver built into an application can directly tell the application whether DNS answers are verified. However, most applications use a stub resolver that relies on a recursive name server to do the verification. The recursive server can use the AD bit to tell the stub resolver (and the application) whether the data is secure. This way, the application does not need to implement the full complexity of DNSSEC validation itself.

The problem is that without cryptographic verification, the AD bit cannot be trusted. An untrusted server can set the bit even for unverified data. Therefore, the AD bit SHOULD only be trusted when the end consumer has explicitly configured the resolver as trustworthy and the communication is protected (for example, via TSIG message authentication or a secure transport like IPsec).
sections.eli5: Your mail or browser app cannot check DNS signatures itself, so it relies on the system DNS server to check them. The AD bit tells the app 'this answer is really checked', but only if you trust that particular server.

sections.title: When Servers Set the AD Bit
sections.content:
Recursive servers (those that do queries on behalf of clients) set the AD bit when all RRsets in the answer section and all relevant negative-proof RRsets in the authority section have been cryptographically verified. The presence of the Checking Disabled (CD) bit in a query does not affect the AD bit in the response; if the requested data has already been verified or meets policy, the AD bit is still set.

Authoritative servers (those that answer for their own zones) MUST be explicitly configured to set the AD bit, and this behavior MUST default to off. An authoritative server MAY set the AD bit for its own zone data if configured to treat the zone as authenticated. Secondary servers SHOULD NOT consider zone data authenticated unless the zone was transferred securely or the data was verified. Iterative resolvers SHOULD ignore the AD bit from authoritative servers.
sections.eli5: A recursive server (the one your app queries) can set the bit after verifying signatures. An authoritative server (the source of the data) can also set it, but should rarely do so. Either way, you should only trust it from a server you have explicitly configured as trustworthy.

sections.title: Interpreting the AD Bit Safely
sections.content:
A resolver MUST NOT blindly trust the AD bit unless it uses a secure transport mechanism (such as IPsec, TLS, or TSIG message authentication) when communicating with the recursive nameserver, and the resolver has been explicitly configured to trust that server. Without these protections, an attacker could spoof the AD bit.

The AD bit is intended for use only by applications that have a trust relationship with the resolver. A home user relying on their ISP's recursive DNS server should not trust the AD bit, because the path to the server is not protected and the ISP may not be trustworthy. When security status matters, running a local resolver or using a explicitly configured trusted resolver is recommended.
sections.eli5: Only trust the checkmark if: you can verify it came from a trusted server (using encryption or signing), you told your system to trust that server, and you are sure the path between you and the server is safe.

sections.title: References and Security
sections.content:
The AD bit MUST only be set if DNSSEC records have been requested via the DO (DNSSEC OK) bit and relevant SIG records are returned. This ensures that the AD bit is only used in DNSSEC-aware communications.

The RFC updates RFC 2535, section 6.1, with the new definition. Authoritative servers can be explicitly configured to set the AD bit without performing cryptographic checks; this behavior is a security risk and MUST be disabled by default. Resolvers that blindly trust the AD bit without knowing the security policy of the server generating the answer cannot be considered security aware. Organizations that require all DNS responses to contain cryptographically verified data should separate authoritative name server functions from DNSSEC verification functions, since name servers are not required to validate signatures for data they serve.
sections.eli5: The checkmark only matters if you asked for DNSSEC signatures (using the DO bit). Be careful: servers can be misconfigured to set the bit without actually checking anything.
